name: Tanning wipes / towelettes

lead: Tanning wipes are pre-moistened cloths impregnated with a self-tanning or bronzing composition, such as DHA, that you wipe over the skin. The payoff is quick, portable bronzed colour without a bottle or mitt.

The chain is the same as other self-tanners: DHA reacts with the dead outer skin layer to give colour without UV, and the colour shows as it develops. A patent filing describes the concept of tissue impregnated with tanning lotion, oil or bronzing agent; no clinical studies of the category were found.

paras: People wipe the cloth over face and body in even strokes, often for travel or touch-ups. Colour develops over hours and fades in about 3 to 10 days.
Uneven wiping can cause streaking or orange colour, and DHA is not approved around eyes, lips or mucous membranes. Bronzers may rub off on clothing.

web.title: How Do You Use Tanning Wipes?

angle.text: You reach for tanning wipes for a quick, portable way to add bronzed colour without a mitt or bottle. DHA or bronzer tints the skin, and the colour shows as it develops. It is temporary and fades within days.

lead: Tanning wipes, or towelettes, are single-use tissues pre-soaked with a self-tanning formula that people rub over the skin to get a sunless tan. They give a bronzed, healthier-looking skin tone without UV exposure, in a pack that is quick and portable. [1][2] The active ingredient is usually dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a sugar-derived compound that colours the outer skin layer. [3]

Brands describe a wipe as providing enough product for the whole body, and L'Oreal's guidance says the colour goes on clear, builds with daily repeat use and lasts about a week. [1][2] A patent filing describes the concept of a tanning aid made of tissue paper impregnated with a tanning lotion, tanning oil or bronzing agent.

Wipes are used mainly on the body; one brand's guidance says they are not meant for the face, suggesting a separate face product or foundation to match. [1] No clinical studies of tanning wipes as a category were found.
infobox: About 3 to 10 days; about a week per brand guidance [3][1]
Body; face not recommended by one brand [1]
Repeat daily to deepen, weekly to maintain, per brand guidance [1]

paras: A patented concept pairs a tissue with an impregnated tanning lotion, oil or bronzing agent, wiped over the body surface.  Wikipedia's sunless tanning article lists creams, lotions, sprays, bronzers and gradual tanners rather than wipes, which are sold by several mainstream brands. [3][2]

Brand guidance describes preparing the skin by exfoliating and moisturising, using less product around knees, elbows, wrists, ankles, hands and feet, rubbing the wipe in broad strokes, washing hands afterward to avoid stained palms, and letting the colour dry before dressing. [1][2] A glow is said to be visible within about 24 hours. [2]

DHA is not a dye. It reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer in a Maillard-type browning reaction that does not need UV light and does not involve the skin's melanin. [3] Colour fades gradually over about 3 to 10 days as that layer sheds. [3]

Eva Wittgenstein noticed in the 1950s at Cincinnati Children's Hospital that DHA used in an oral treatment stained the skin brown. [3] Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner, appeared in 1959 and Coppertone's Quick Tan in 1960, and automated spray booths broadened the market from the late 1990s. [3] Wipes are a later convenience format of the same chemistry; a patent publication describes the concept.

Improper application is reported to produce orange or splotchy colour, and brand guidance mentions palm staining and a strong DHA smell. [3][1][2] The FDA has approved DHA for external use but not near the eyes, lips or mucous membranes. [3]

Wikipedia notes that DHA-treated skin showed more free radicals under sun exposure in a 2007 study, mainly a concern for about 24 hours after application, and that sunscreen in tanning products fades before the tan does. [3] DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis. [3]

No studies found on tanning wipes. Wikipedia's sunless tanning article summarises laboratory and clinical research on DHA more broadly, including the 2007 free-radical study and a cell-culture study reporting DNA damage. [3]
